## Oaxaca on foot: exploring the historic center

[Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) is one of those Mexican cities best discovered on foot. Streets lined with low-rise facades, former convent complexes, squares, workshops, and markets are all found in its historic heart. Ada Tours offers a **four-hour guided sightseeing tour** that introduces Oaxaca's history and the principal landmarks of its center.

The itinerary includes **Santo Domingo Church**, a walk along **Andador Turístico**, and the **Zócalo**, the city's main square. The focus extends beyond the buildings: your guide explains the region's pre-Hispanic heritage, the period of Spanish rule, and its living cultural traditions.

UNESCO's official listing combines **the historic center of Oaxaca and the archaeological site of Monte Albán**. Both belong to the history of the region but stand in different locations. This walking tour focuses primarily on **the city center**; Ada Tours offers a separate excursion to the ancient archaeological site.

## Santo Domingo: Baroque architecture and city history

The **Church of Santo Domingo de Guzmán** is among Oaxaca's most recognizable architectural monuments. Its facade and interior reflect Mexico's colonial history. Parts of the former convent complex stand beside it.

As you explore, notice the building's composition, ornamental details, and place within the surrounding streets. The guide connects religious architecture with the city's social history and urban development. A church appearing on the itinerary does not mean every room is open on any given day: services and access restrictions may change how the visit proceeds.

Oaxaca is in a seismically active region, and its historic architecture was designed with earthquakes in mind. UNESCO specifically notes the sturdy walls and relatively low buildings of the historic center.

## Andador Turístico: crafts, galleries, and cafés

**Andador Turístico** is a pedestrian street lined with small shops, galleries, cafés, and buildings with characteristic facades. It is an ideal place to notice details of everyday urban life that are easy to miss from a vehicle.

On the walk, you can discover the work of local craftspeople, including textiles, ceramics, wooden objects, and other creations. Even without shopping, it is rewarding to see the range of materials used by Oaxaca's artisans.

Additional purchases and café tastings are not included: under the Ada Tours terms, **meals and personal expenses are paid separately**.

## The Zócalo and markets: Oaxaca's public life

The **Zócalo** is the central square and a place for walks and gatherings. It offers a chance to see how the historic street plan continues to serve everyday life. We also visit **markets and squares**, discovering local crafts and customs.

One of the most valuable parts of the walk is hearing your guide discuss the region's Indigenous peoples, the historical roles of the Zapotec and Mixtec, the influence of the Spanish period, and the development of the modern city. Oaxaca's culture draws on many traditions and cannot be reduced to one costume or one dish.

Travelers drawn to the city's history may also enjoy Ada Tours' [selection of cultural journeys](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## What the excursion includes and how long it lasts

Our excursion includes the following:

| Detail | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| Duration | 4 hours |
| Start | 9:00–9:30 |
| Languages | English, Spanish |
| Included | Shared transport, guide, admission |
| Paid separately | Meals, tips, personal expenses |

A **certified bilingual guide** and **admission to historic sites** are part of the program. **Shared transport** is also provided, but this does not turn the experience into a continuous driving tour: most of the itinerary is on foot through the historic center.

**Meals, admission to optional attractions, tips, and personal expenses** are not included. Admission to historic sites covers the main route; additional visits outside it must be arranged separately.

The price of a standalone excursion is agreed upon when booking. Ask for the rate applicable to your chosen date and group size.

## What you can add after the walk

The itinerary mentions optional cultural activities: **a cooking class**, visits to art galleries, and **a tasting of mezcal from a local producer**. These are potential additions after the main walk, not mandatory parts of the four-hour tour.

For a deeper introduction to local crafts, see the separate [eight-hour Monte Albán and artisan villages excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/). It includes [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/) and [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/), known for their alebrije figures and black-clay pottery.

This combination works well on a multi-day journey around [Mexico](/mexico/): one day introduces the city, and another explores the hilltop monument and workshops outside the center.

## Preparing for a city walk

Comfortable shoes, sun protection, and drinking water are useful for exploring the pedestrian center. During warm hours, shaded passages between buildings may give way to open squares. When visiting religious buildings, respect rules about clothing, photography, and access.

The tour is scheduled to start in the morning, leaving free time after the main activity. Additional experiences need to be arranged individually; they are not automatically included in the four-hour route.

## Frequently asked questions about sightseeing in Oaxaca

### How long does the excursion last?

**4 hours.** The published description gives a starting time of **9:00–9:30 a.m.**

### Does the tour visit Monte Albán?

No. This tour focuses on **Oaxaca's historic city center**. A separate [Monte Albán and artisan villages excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/) covers the archaeological site.

### What languages is the tour conducted in?

**English and Spanish** are confirmed. Russian is not listed among the standard services.

### Is a cooking class or mezcal tasting included?

No. The cooking experience, galleries, and tasting are described as **possible optional activities** after the walk.

### Are entrance tickets included?

The program includes **admission to the historic sites on the main route**. Tickets for additional optional attractions are not included.

## Tours featuring the Oaxaca sightseeing walk: which should you choose?

[Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) brings together pre-Columbian history, colonial architecture, and lively city markets. Walking is a good way to begin: the main streets and squares of the historic center are relatively close together. The Ada Tours excursion lasts about **4 hours**, combining Santo Domingo Church, the pedestrian Andador Turístico, Zócalo Square, and an introduction to daily life in the city.

The same [Oaxaca city walking route](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) is used in two multi-day itineraries. They differ in overall duration, neighboring days, and the opportunity to see other Mexican states.

| Journey | Oaxaca excursion |
|---|---|
| [Oaxaca, 5 days](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) | Day 2, the foundation of the cultural program |
| [Viva Mexico, 12 days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) | Day 6, one part of a journey through Mexico |

If you want to explore one region at a relaxed pace, compare the number of nights in Oaxaca rather than counting the attractions in a promotional headline. The five-day program includes four nights in one city. On the longer 12-day itinerary, Oaxaca is an important but intermediate stop.

## Five days in Oaxaca: the city center and surrounding region

On the [short Oaxaca tour](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/), day two begins with a guided sightseeing walk. It helps visitors get their bearings before traveling farther afield. Day three features [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/), the ancient Zapotec ceremonial complex, followed by the artisan villages of [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/) and [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/).

Day four explores more of the region's culture through Mitla, the textiles of Teotitlán del Valle, Hierve el Agua, and other places. The main advantage of the five-day itinerary is this coherent regional program. Places and traditions introduced during the city walk can later be explored at archaeological monuments and artisan workshops.

A shorter tour does not mean every service is private. Under its terms, airport transfers are private, while the excursions on days two through four are shared. The guide is certified, with English and Spanish offered. Accommodation with breakfast is included; additional cultural activities and some expenses are paid separately.

## Viva Mexico: Oaxaca as one stage of a larger journey

The [12-day Viva Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) covers Mexico City, Oaxaca, and the Yucatán. Its walking tour of Oaxaca's historic center takes place on **day six**. The next day, the itinerary continues to Monte Albán and artisan workshops.

This option suits visitors who want a broad first introduction to Mexico. One journey brings together historic towns, archaeology, and natural attractions in different regions. However, the schedule is busier: transfers and flights take time, and the opportunity for independent walks in each city is limited.

Viva Mexico includes standard accommodation with breakfast, shared excursions and transfers, tickets to the specified historical attractions, and the services of a bilingual guide. Flights, additional meals, tips, and personal expenses are paid separately. If you want a slower-paced experience of Oaxaca with independent visits to galleries and markets, the five-day route may be more suitable.

## What is included in the four-hour excursion?

The approximate starting time is **9:00–9:30**. During the walk, travelers discover Oaxaca's historic center, which is listed by UNESCO together with the archaeological site of Monte Albán. One of the main architectural landmarks is Santo Domingo Church, associated with the history of the Dominican order in the city.

Andador Turístico is a pedestrian street with artisan shops, galleries, and cafés. Zócalo Square remains a public gathering place where visitors can observe daily life, including meetings, trade, and locals strolling around. Along the way, the guide explains how Zapotec and Mixtec traditions, Spanish colonial heritage, and local artistic practices come together in Oaxaca's contemporary culture.

The excursion includes shared transportation, a certified bilingual guide, and admission to the listed historical sites. Meals, personal expenses, tips, and admission to optional attractions are not included. This is a guided sightseeing walk, so do not expect extended visits to every art gallery in the city.

## Cooking class, galleries, and mezcal: possible additions

After the main excursion, we offer optional cultural activities: a cooking workshop, visits to art galleries, or a mezcal tasting with a local producer. These are **possible extensions**, not three included activities that every participant automatically experiences.

If gastronomy is your interest, find out in advance which activity can be arranged on your date and how much time you will have after the walk. Gallery visits depend on opening hours; an artisan workshop depends on the craftsperson's schedule. Free time on one itinerary does not guarantee the same opportunity on another.

You can also explore the separate [Monte Albán and artisan villages excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/). It occupies a full sightseeing day and differs from the shorter city walking tour.

## Choosing the right travel pace

For a walking day, bring comfortable shoes, a hat, and water. Oaxaca's center is best discovered on foot, but there are cobbled streets and areas exposed to the sun. Travelers with limited mobility should discuss accessibility along the specific route with the organizer in advance.

The five-day program offers several consecutive days in one region without repeated hotel changes. The 12-day trip is better suited to those who want to see several cultural regions in one journey. In both cases, the historic-center excursion is described as being guided in English or Spanish.

Choose your trip from the [Mexico tour catalog](/mexico/tour/). Inclusion of the excursion is confirmed by the tour's specific link to the [Oaxaca sightseeing route](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/), rather than merely by the fact that the journey passes through the city.

## Frequently asked questions about tours with an Oaxaca excursion

### How long is the historic-center walk?

The standalone excursion takes around four hours, starting at 9:00–9:30. On the five-day itinerary, it takes place on day two; on the 12-day itinerary, on day six.

### Does the same tour include Monte Albán?

Yes. Both named itineraries also include a separate [excursion to Monte Albán](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/). It takes place on another day and is not part of the four-hour walk.

### Are the cooking class and mezcal tasting included?

The walking tour description lists them as additional possibilities after the excursion. Their inclusion and price must be arranged separately.

### Can I request the tour with a Russian-speaking guide?

The standard itinerary lists English and Spanish. Russian-language guiding requires separate confirmation and is not included by default.

### How do the two tour options differ?

[Five days in Oaxaca](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) focus on one region and its surroundings. [Twelve days on Viva Mexico](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) combine Oaxaca with Mexico City and the Yucatán, but involve more transfers.

## Visiting Ocotlán Basilica: pilgrimage and Baroque art in Tlaxcala

The [Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) is located near Tlaxcala city in central Mexico. It is recognizable by its two tall red-brick towers, intricately carved light-colored facade, and richly decorated Baroque interior. The sanctuary is significant both to pilgrims and to visitors interested in colonial architecture.

The name often causes confusion: this Ocotlán is **near Tlaxcala**, not Ocotlán de Morelos in Oaxaca state. That distinction matters when choosing an itinerary: the basilica is part of a pilgrimage day in central Mexico.

## Which Ada Tours excursion includes the basilica?

On our current [Sanctuaries of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán, and Puebla](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/) itinerary, the basilica is an important stop. The route covers several places of worship and historic cities; visiting Ocotlán on this particular product should not be understood as a short standalone excursion.

The day's sequence is:

1. [San Miguel del Milagro Sanctuary](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/) and a Holy Mass.
2. [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/) and a visit to the San Francisco convent.
3. [Ocotlán Basilica](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/), including its altar and venerated image of Our Lady.
4. [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/), with the cathedral, Santo Domingo Church, and the Chapel of the Rosary.

The itinerary returns to Mexico City. We offer it as a **private excursion** with an English-speaking guide. Private transport, guiding, admission to the listed sights, and one Mass are included. A separately fixed price, an exact duration in hours, and a Russian-speaking guide have not been confirmed for this excursion.

## What to look for inside the sanctuary

The basilica's exterior is a characteristic example of Mexican Baroque, with particularly expressive facade decoration. Take time to examine not only the towers but also the portal, where white stucco contrasts with brickwork.

Inside, the main focus is the altar with the image of Our Lady of Ocotlán. Another notable space is the *Camarín*, a special room associated with dressing the venerated statue for religious ceremonies. A visit makes it possible to connect the sanctuary's architectural design with its continuing devotional tradition.

According to Catholic tradition, Ocotlán's story is linked to an apparition of the Virgin Mary in 1541 and the discovery of a wooden image inside a tree. This is a **religious tradition** and should be presented as a matter of faith and local history, not as a miraculously proven event.

## How Ocotlán differs from the other stops that day

[San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/) is associated above all with the pilgrimage Mass and devotion to the Archangel Michael. Tlaxcala introduces early colonial monuments. At Ocotlán, the focus is on the image of Our Lady, Baroque decoration, and the history of the sanctuary. Puebla concludes the sequence of churches with a larger ensemble of urban architecture.

The day suits travelers interested in the religious and artistic history of central Mexico. If your aim is to study the interior of one basilica in depth, discuss the overall pace and access to individual rooms before choosing this itinerary: the listed stops go well beyond a single church.

## Preparing for the pilgrimage route

The day combines travel between cities, visits to active churches, and participation in a religious service. Comfortable footwear for stone floors and historic quarters, modest clothing for places of worship, and enough time for stops along the way are practical considerations. Photography and independent movement may be restricted during services.

Tell us whether participating in Mass, seeing the Camarín, and spending time at the main altar are particularly important to you. Access to specific parts of the sanctuary and the schedule of religious events must be checked for your chosen date; constant access to every room cannot be guaranteed.

## Frequently asked questions about the Ocotlán excursion

### Is Ocotlán Basilica in Oaxaca?

No. The [Sanctuary of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) is near Tlaxcala. The name is shared with places elsewhere in Mexico, so Tlaxcala is the location to look for.

### Can I visit just the basilica without Puebla?

On our [Ada Tours excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/), Ocotlán is part of a route through Tlaxcala and Puebla. This listing does not offer a separate, shorter product; individual changes can be discussed before booking.

### Is Mass included?

Yes. The pilgrimage excursion includes one Holy Mass along the route, at San Miguel del Milagro Sanctuary. This does not mean the service necessarily takes place at Ocotlán.

### Is the route suitable for someone interested in architecture but not pilgrimage?

Yes, provided the visitor is comfortable entering active religious sites and making several stops in one day. The basilica is noted for Baroque architecture, while Tlaxcala and Puebla offer other monuments of the colonial era.

## Visiting the Old Archbishop's Palace in Mexico City

The [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/) stands on Moneda Street in Mexico City's historic center, near the main Zócalo square. The site connects several eras: its pre-Hispanic past, the early Catholic history of New Spain, and the city's present-day museum life.

We include the palace in a tour of Mexico City's churches and historic sites. It is best understood as a cultural and pilgrimage route, not as a separately promised extended visit to every museum hall in the palace.

## Which itinerary includes the palace?

On our current [Mexico City Churches, Mass, and Garibaldi Square excursion](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/), the day begins at the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/). A Holy Mass at [Santo Domingo Church](/mexico/place/santo-domingo-mexico-city/) follows. The route then takes in [Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), the National Palace, the Old Archbishop's Palace, and [Garibaldi Square](/mexico/place/garibaldi-plaza/), known for its mariachi performances.

The tour includes **private transport**, an English-speaking guide, and one Mass as part of the pilgrimage itinerary. Admission to the listed attractions is named among the included services. An exact duration in hours and guaranteed access arrangements for all the palace's interior spaces have not been specified.

The National Palace has a particular limitation: it is an active government building, and visitor access may be suspended for official events. A visit cannot be promised unconditionally just because the stop appears on the itinerary.

## Why the Old Archbishop's Palace is worth seeing

The building is associated with Mexico City's first archbishop, Juan de Zumárraga, and the history of the Catholic Church in New Spain. Over time, the residence developed into a substantial palace complex. Its facades and courtyards illustrate colonial architecture in one of the capital's oldest districts.

Today it houses the **Museo de Arte de la Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público**, the art museum of Mexico's Ministry of Finance. The site also has an archaeological dimension: part of the complex occupies the location of a pre-Hispanic temple of Tezcatlipoca, and archaeological viewing windows at the museum reveal earlier layers of construction.

For travelers, it is a rare opportunity to consider the history of the Aztec city, the church administration of the colonial period, and a contemporary art exhibition at the same site. However, an interest in the collection should be distinguished from confirmed access to the galleries on your chosen excursion.

## Including the palace in a walk around the center

The palace lies within the walkable historic center, so it makes the most sense to see it alongside the Zócalo, the cathedral, and nearby churches. This makes it easier to understand why religious and administrative buildings cluster around the main city square.

If Mexico City's religious history is your priority, the route with Mass at Santo Domingo is suitable. If you are most interested in the art museum, archaeological windows, and inner courtyards, check that those specific spaces can be visited. Regular museum opening hours do not guarantee that an excursion group will have access to every room.

For a broader journey around the country, compare [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/). General information on the country's history, geography, and travel seasons is available on our [Mexico page](/mexico/).

## What to check before traveling

Ask us about the actual sequence of stops and the museum's entry conditions. Religious services and official events may affect access along parts of the route. The program combines working churches, a museum, and a lively city square, so tell us in advance if you prefer a slower pace and how much time you would like to spend inside the buildings.

Do not confuse the Old Archbishop's Palace with the National Palace: these are different historic buildings near the central square, with different functions and visiting regulations.

## Frequently asked questions about the Archbishop's Palace

### Where is the Old Archbishop's Palace?

In Mexico City's historic center, at **4 Moneda Street**, near the Zócalo. Its dedicated [place page](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/) helps distinguish it from neighboring palaces.

### Is it a church building or a museum?

Historically, this was the archbishops' residence. Today the palace is known as an art museum operated by Mexico's Ministry of Finance. The excursion can therefore discuss both church history and the building's architecture.

### Is entry to the museum halls guaranteed?

No. Current access arrangements and the content of the specific excursion need to be checked for your chosen date. Listing the palace as a stop does not itself confirm that every exhibition will be visited.

### Does the palace feature on the itinerary with a Mass?

Yes. The [Mexico City pilgrimage excursion](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/) includes the Archbishop's Palace after the churches and cathedral; one Mass is scheduled at Santo Domingo Church.

## Visiting the Palace of Cortés in Cuernavaca: Morelos history and the road to Taxco

The [Palace of Cortés](/mexico/place/palace-of-cortes/) stands in central Cuernavaca in the Mexican state of Morelos. This imposing 16th-century stone building is associated with Hernán Cortés and the region's early colonial history. Today it houses the Regional Museum of the Peoples of Morelos, dedicated to the area's history and culture from precolonial times to the present.

We include the palace in our [Cuernavaca, Taxco, and Mass at Santa Prisca excursion](/mexico/cuernavaca/cuernavaca-taxco-pilgrimage/). The itinerary combines Cuernavaca's architecture with a visit to Taxco and a religious program. It is a **private excursion with an English-speaking guide**, not a standalone museum ticket or a self-guided walk devoted only to the palace.

## What to see at the Palace of Cortés

The building stands out for its massive stone walls and the appearance of a fortified residence. The palace dates from the first decades of the Spanish colonial period. It later served several purposes; its historic interiors are now used as museum galleries.

Exhibitions at the Regional Museum of the Peoples of Morelos explore pre-Hispanic cultures, the history of the conquest, the colonial period, and the region's social life. Visitors can see archaeological artifacts, historical records, and works of art. This provides a much broader understanding of Cuernavaca than a single episode in the life of Cortés.

The palace's architecture is also interesting in its own right. Its rugged stone facades, imposing form, and central location allow visitors to compare 16th-century civic buildings with neighboring religious structures.

## How the palace fits into the Ada Tours excursion

The [private Cuernavaca and Taxco tour](/mexico/cuernavaca/cuernavaca-taxco-pilgrimage/) begins with a journey to Cuernavaca, known for its mild climate. Stops include the Palace of Cortés and Cuernavaca Cathedral, associated with a former 16th-century Franciscan convent.

The route then continues to **Taxco**, a historic town known for silversmithing and colonial architecture. The principal architectural landmark on this program is Santa Prisca Church, an outstanding Baroque building. One Holy Mass is scheduled there.

It is important to distinguish the stops: **Mass takes place at Santa Prisca in Taxco**, while the Palace of Cortés is a cultural stop in Cuernavaca. There is no basis for suggesting the service takes place in the palace or museum.

## What the excursion includes

The tour includes private transport, an English-speaking guide, admission tickets to the listed attractions, and **one Holy Mass along the route**.

An exact departure time, price, and duration have not been specified for this excursion. Nor can access to every museum exhibition on a particular day be guaranteed: opening hours and temporary restrictions depend on the institutions.

If the palace's museum collections are your main interest, discuss in advance how much time will be spent in Cuernavaca. The itinerary also includes the cathedral and a substantial drive to Taxco, so a museum stop is not the same as a full day inside the building.

## Preparing for the visit

Comfortable everyday shoes are suitable for the city section, which passes through the historic center and may include cobbled streets. Modest clothing is appropriate in religious buildings. In hot months, sun protection and drinking water are useful.

Check the regional museum's opening times and photography rules against its current regulations. Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) maintains the museum's official page. Individual museum concessions and admission rates should not be confused with the Ada Tours excursion package, which already lists entrance tickets for the scheduled visits.

For a broader introduction to the country's colonial heritage, explore [cultural and historical journeys in Mexico](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/).

## Frequently asked questions about the Palace of Cortés

### Can I visit the palace on the same excursion as Taxco?

Yes. On the [Ada Tours itinerary](/mexico/cuernavaca/cuernavaca-taxco-pilgrimage/), the Palace of Cortés is visited in Cuernavaca before continuing to Taxco.

### Is admission included?

Entrance tickets for the listed attractions are included in the private excursion. The museum's actual opening hours should be checked separately.

### Where does the Mass take place?

At Santa Prisca Church in Taxco. The Palace of Cortés is the museum and historical site visited at another stop.
